entities.summary:
Fabrizio Paolucci (1651–1726) was a highly influential Italian cardinal and statesman in the Roman Catholic Church, serving as Papal Secretary of State for over two decades under two popes. His career spanned the late 17th and early 18th centuries, a period marked by intense European dynastic conflicts, notably the War of the Spanish Succession, which profoundly impacted the geopolitical standing of the Papal States. Paolucci's enduring significance lies in his sustained diplomatic efforts to maintain papal sovereignty and influence amidst the shifting power dynamics of Bourbon France, Habsburg Austria, and other European powers, making him a central figure in the curial administration of the Early Modern era.

Born in Forlì on April 22, 1651, Paolucci rose through the ecclesiastical ranks, holding significant administrative and diplomatic posts, including Governor of Rome and Apostolic Nuncio to Cologne. Elevated to cardinal by Pope Innocent XII in 1697, he became a close advisor to Pope Clement XI, who appointed him Secretary of State in 1700. In this capacity, Paolucci managed the Holy See's foreign policy through the protracted War of the Spanish Succession (1701-1714), navigating complex alliances and territorial disputes, often clashing with imperial ambitions. He was considered a strong candidate for the papacy in the conclaves of 1721 and 1724, though ultimately unsuccessful. He returned to the Secretary of State role under Pope Benedict XIII from 1724 until his death.
